name: Man
baseMeaning: A man emoji: a smiling man with short blond hair, cropped at the shoulders.
tldr: Man 👨: referring to a man, often a third party.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — referring to a man, often a third party — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: a smiling man with short blond hair, cropped at the shoulders. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker 👨

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as referring to a man, often a third party.
contextMeanings.example: Replying to a thread about a man 👨

contextMeanings.meaning: Used sarcastically it is the gesture with the deadpan delivery: referring to a man, often a third party, said without believing any of it.

platformNotes.note: In TikTok comments 👨 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays referring to a man, often a third party, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 👨 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 👨 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its referring to a man, often a third party reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 👨 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like replying to a thread about a man. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Man 👨 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

generationalNotes.note: Older senders use 👨 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the referring to a man, often a third party subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for 👨 to do the work of mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is referring to a man, often a third party.

Millennials tend to send 👨 deliberately, usually for something like replying to a thread about a man, and they read referring to a man, often a third party into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 👨 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read referring to a man, often a third party into it than younger senders are.

warnings.title: 👨 and 🧑 get swapped
warnings.description: The Person 🧑 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the neutral person covers anyone, the man emoji is one man and gets read as gendered by default. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 👨 as something else fairly often: it gets used as a generic stand-in for a person, when the base emoji is explicitly male and a separate neutral option exists — a mismatch can quietly put words in the men’s mouths. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 👨 Man Emoji Meaning and How to Use It
seoDescription: What 👨 means when people send it, the man reading, and how to answer it without guessing.

longForm.overview:
What follows is the useful part: the two things the man is actually for (mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker and replying to a thread about a man), the reading it gets when it is not what the sender meant, and the five tone pages that sit under this one.

There is not a lot to the picture. 👨 is a smiling man with short blond hair, cropped at the shoulders, added in Unicode 13.0 and filed under person. What it does in a message is carry a meaning — here, referring to a man, often a third party — without anyone having to write it out.

That plain reading is the one most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture is doing the same work as the sentence it replaces, and it lands first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets used as a generic stand-in for a person, when the base emoji is explicitly male and a separate neutral option exists — a mismatch can quietly put words in the men’s mouths. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🧑 Person: the neutral person covers anyone, the man emoji is one man and gets read as gendered by default. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

There are five tone versions of this emoji, and they are not copies of this page. Each one describes the same gesture from inside a different group, because a tone is read as a signal about the sender before the sentence is read.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The common uses are mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker and replying to a thread about a man. The first one is about speed — the picture replaces the explanation, and it lands before the words would have. The second is about tone — the sentence stands on its own, and the emoji is there to change how it reads.

The same emoji in three rooms: a family thread, a work channel, and a dating app. In the first it closes a conversation, in the second it hands something over, in the third it is a joke with an eyebrow raised. The drawing never changes; the expectation of the reader does.

That is also the reason the skin-tone variants are written as their own pages rather than as one page with a table of swatches. A tone is not a setting, and it is read differently.

Look at how often 👨 is used to avoid typing. A question goes out, a question comes back, and in between there is a single picture standing in for an answer that would have taken a sentence. It reads as "referring to a man, often a third party", which is fine until it is not.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Watch the picker, and watch the thread. 👨 is easy to send when 🧑 Person was meant — the neutral person covers anyone, the man emoji is one man and gets read as gendered by default. And the emoji has no business being the whole reply to somebody who has just told you something bad: it reads as "referring to a man, often a third party", which is about the gesture rather than about them.

The problem is not the emoji, it is the message underneath it. 👨 gets used as a generic stand-in for a person, when the base emoji is explicitly male and a separate neutral option exists — a mismatch can quietly put words in the men’s mouths, and the drift happens silently. Nobody notices that the meaning changed, because the change was in a picture.

Nor is it a good opener with a stranger. The drawing is cold, and man gestures have collected a faintly superior edge from being used to reply to other people for years.

Professional settings are the other place to leave it alone. Put 👨 next to somebody's performance, or in a first note to a client, and referring to a man, often a third party is the note it reads as — a note that costs more in a workplace than in a group chat.
longForm.howToReply:
Matching works when the message was a reaction: send 👨 back and the tone is confirmed without a word. It does not work when the message was aimed at you. A request, a handover, a nudge — those want a sentence, because two gestures in a row leave the question open.

If you cannot tell how the man was meant, read the line above it instead. 👨 gets used as a generic stand-in for a person, when the base emoji is explicitly male and a separate neutral option exists — a mismatch can quietly put words in the men’s mouths; the sentence underneath is the part that disambiguates it.

Warmth needs words next to the picture. Something like mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker sent with 👨 on its own is a coin toss between referring to a man, often a third party and something sharper, and the sender never gets to pick which one landed.

faqs.question: What does 👨 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👨 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under man show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 👨 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 👨 is used for referring to a man, often a third party. The drawing shows a smiling man with short blond hair, cropped at the shoulders, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👨 and 🧑?
faqs.answer: The neutral person covers anyone, the man emoji is one man and gets read as gendered by default. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 👨 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as referring to a man, often a third party, but it gets used as a generic stand-in for a person, when the base emoji is explicitly male and a separate neutral option exists — a mismatch can quietly put words in the men’s mouths. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

conversationExamples.message: mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker 👨
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is referring to a man, often a third party, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: mentioning a friend, a dad, or a coworker 👨
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as referring to a man, often a third party, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: replying to a thread about a man 👨
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as referring to a man, often a third party, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 👨
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets used as a generic stand-in for a person, when the base emoji is explicitly male and a separate neutral option exists — a mismatch can quietly put words in the men’s mouths more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.
